reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented company renews 120 certificates a year, each with reminders sent to one person's mailbox. Assume each renewal has a 2% chance of being missed under that arrangement, and that expiry monitoring with alerts to a team at 30, 14 and 7 days cuts that chance to 0.1%. The probabilities are illustrative.

Derivation: with personal reminders, the expected number of missed renewals is 120 × 0.02 = 2.4 a year. Correcting the one person involved changes almost nothing, because the other 119 certificates keep the same weakness. With team-routed monitoring, the expectation falls to 120 × 0.001 = 0.12 a year.

Independent check: list why the expiry was possible: reminders tied to individuals, no inventory linking certificates to teams, no monitoring of expiry dates and manual renewal. None of these is a person's character; each is a condition that will catch the next person too.

Misconception to reject: 'blameless means nobody is accountable.' Accountability moves from punishing the past to owning the future: each action item, such as the expiry alerting or a certificate inventory, gets a named owner and a due date, and someone checks that it closes.

Change one factor: add automated renewal for the 100 certificates whose issuer supports it. If the remaining 20 stay on monitored manual renewal at 0.1%, the expectation becomes about 20 × 0.001 = 0.02 missed renewals a year, assuming automated renewal is close to never missed.

The scenario and probabilities are invented.

leadership-error-budget.essentialQuestion: A service with a 99.95% quarterly availability objective has already had 40 minutes of downtime this quarter. How much error budget remains, and should a migration expected to cause 30 minutes of downtime go ahead this quarter?

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented service measured over a 90-day quarter with an availability objective of 99.95%. Two incidents have used 22 and 18 minutes. A planned database migration is expected to cause about 30 minutes of downtime. Downtime is counted in whole minutes and partial degradation is ignored.

Derivation: the quarter has 90 × 24 × 60 = 129,600 minutes, and 0.05% of that is 64.8 minutes of allowed downtime. After 22 + 18 = 40 minutes, the remaining budget is 64.8 − 40 = 24.8 minutes, about 38% of the total. The migration's 30 minutes would exceed it by about 5 minutes.
Independent check: 99.95% of 129,600 minutes is 129,535.2 minutes of required uptime, and 129,600 − 129,535.2 = 64.8 minutes, which matches the budget computed directly.

Misconception to reject: 'every minute of downtime is a failure, so the target should be 100%.' The SRE book argues that 100% is the wrong reliability target for basically everything; the budget exists so that risky but valuable work, such as this migration, can be planned against an explicit allowance.

Change one factor: with a 99.9% objective, the quarter allows 129.6 minutes, 89.6 remain after the incidents and the migration fits. The team could also keep the 99.95% objective and reduce the migration's expected downtime, for example by moving it to a design with a shorter cutover.

Source and limits: chapter 3 of Google's Site Reliability Engineering book, 'Embracing Risk', describes the error budget: product management sets an objective for the quarter, monitoring measures actual uptime and the difference is the unreliability still available: https://sre.google/sre-book/embracing-risk/. All the figures here are invented.

leadership-runbook.essentialQuestion: A routine certificate rotation has 12 manual steps. Why does a runbook with a check after every step make the procedure much safer, and what else must the runbook contain?

leadership-runbook.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented procedure with 12 manual steps. Assume each step has a 1% chance of an unnoticed mistake and that mistakes are independent. A runbook adds an observable check after each step that catches 90% of mistakes, leaving 0.1% per step. These probabilities are illustrative, not measured.

Derivation: without checks, the chance that all 12 steps go right is 0.99^12 ≈ 0.886, so about 11.4% of runs contain at least one mistake. With checks, it is 0.999^12 ≈ 0.988, so about 1.19% of runs contain an uncaught mistake, roughly a tenth as many.

Independent check: for small probabilities, the chance of at least one mistake is close to the number of steps times the per-step chance: 12 × 1% = 12% and 12 × 0.1% = 1.2%. Both approximations sit just above the exact values, as they should.

Misconception to reject: 'experienced operators don't need a runbook.' Experience lowers the per-step error rate but does not remove it, and the risk grows with the number of steps. A runbook also records the prerequisites, the points where an operator must stop and decide, who to escalate to and how to roll back.
Change one factor: with 24 steps, the unchecked chance of at least one mistake rises to about 21.4% and the checked chance to about 2.37%. Longer procedures need checks more, or should be automated.

Source and limits: chapter 1 of Google's Site Reliability Engineering book reports that recording best practices ahead of time in a playbook produces roughly a 3x improvement in mean time to repair compared with improvising: https://sre.google/sre-book/introduction/. That figure is Google's experience; the error rates and the independence assumption here are invented.

leadership-service-owner.essentialQuestion: A service is built by one team and run by another, and most pages end up escalated back to the builders. What does single ownership of the whole outcome change, and what must the owner be responsible for?
leadership-service-owner.verifiedBoundary: Service ownership assigns clear accountability for reliability, lifecycle, risk, documentation, and improvement of a technology service.
leadership-service-owner.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: A payroll integration has an owner who tracks vendor changes, certificates, monitoring, business calendar constraints, and recovery procedures. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented service gets 14 pages a month. The operations team that receives them must escalate 10 of the 14 to the development team, and each escalation adds about 25 minutes before the right person is working on the problem. The figures are illustrative.

Derivation: escalation delay costs 10 × 25 = 250 minutes of response time a month. If the team that builds the service also receives its pages, that delay disappears, and the people who can change the code feel every recurring page, which gives them a reason to remove its cause.

Independent check: list the outcomes that need an owner: reliability against the service's objective, lifecycle and upgrades, risk and security, documentation and runbooks, and improvement. With split ownership, each item has two partial owners and the gaps sit between them; with one owner, each item has a name.

Misconception to reject: 'shared ownership means everyone owns it.' When everyone owns an outcome, no one is accountable for its gaps; single ownership does not mean working alone, since the owner can still rely on platform and operations teams for help.

Change one factor: if only 4 of the 14 pages needed the builders' expertise, the delay saved would be 4 × 25 = 100 minutes a month. The case for moving pages depends on how many truly need the code's authors, which you can count from the page history.

Source and limits: in 'A Conversation with Werner Vogels', ACM Queue 4(4), 2006, Amazon's CTO describes the model 'you build it, you run it' and says giving developers operational responsibilities greatly enhanced service quality and put them in day-to-day contact with customers: https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=1142065. That is one company's experience reported in an interview, not a controlled study; the page counts are invented.

leadership-capacity.essentialQuestion: Peak traffic is 6,000 requests per second, growing 4% a month, a marketing launch will add 1,500 more, and new servers take three months to arrive. How many servers should you plan for, and which inputs must be measured rather than guessed?
leadership-capacity.verifiedBoundary: Capacity planning estimates future demand and ensures enough resources exist to meet service objectives during normal growth and expected failures.
leadership-capacity.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: Plan for peak demand plus the failures you claim the system can tolerate.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: An N+1 cluster must handle peak traffic even with one node unavailable; otherwise redundancy exists on paper but not under load. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented service. Peak demand is 6,000 requests per second (rps), organic growth is 4% a month, procurement takes 3 months, so the forecast looks 6 months ahead, beyond the lead time. A planned launch adds 1,500 rps of peak demand. A load test shows one server handles 800 rps within the latency objective.

Derivation: organic demand in 6 months is 6,000 × 1.04^6 ≈ 7,591.9 rps. Adding the launch gives about 9,091.9 rps. Dividing by 800 rps per server gives 11.36, so 12 servers carry the peak. Planning to survive one server failing while another is down for maintenance adds 2, for 14.
Independent check month by month: 6,000 grows to 6,240.0, 6,489.6, 6,749.2, 7,019.2, 7,299.9 and 7,591.9 rps, which matches the compound-growth result.

Misconception to reject: 'plan from today's average load.' Capacity must meet the peak, forecast beyond the time it takes to add capacity, and include known one-off demand such as launches, which an organic trend cannot see.

Change one factor: a new load test shows a dependency slowed down and one server now handles 650 rps. The peak then needs 9,091.9 / 650 ≈ 13.99, so 14 servers, and 16 with the same failure allowance. The per-server number comes from measurement, so it must be retested regularly.

Source and limits: chapter 1 of Google's Site Reliability Engineering book lists three mandatory steps for capacity planning: an organic demand forecast that extends beyond the lead time for acquiring capacity, the incorporation of inorganic demand sources, and regular load testing to relate raw capacity to service capacity: https://sre.google/sre-book/introduction/. The growth rate, launch size and server capacity here are invented, and the two-server failure allowance is a design choice, not a rule from the book.

leadership-escalation.verifiedBoundary: Escalation brings additional authority, expertise, or urgency into a problem while preserving clear responsibility for follow-through.
leadership-escalation.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented escalation path. The on-call engineer owns the response. After 30 minutes without a diagnosis, or at once if customers are affected, the service's team lead joins. At 2 hours, or at once for the highest severity, the director is informed. Disputes over the error-budget policy go to the CTO. The times are illustrative.

Derivation: an incident that starts at 09:00 and is not yet customer-visible reaches the team lead at 09:30 and the director at 11:00 if it is still unresolved. Each step adds expertise or decision authority, but the incident commander keeps running the response.

Independent check: replay an invented quarter of 12 escalations. If ad-hoc escalation took about 45 minutes to find the right person and a written path takes about 10 minutes, the path saves 12 × 35 = 420 minutes, or 7 hours of incident time, in that quarter.

Misconception to reject: 'escalating means handing the problem off' or 'escalating is admitting failure.' Escalation brings in people who can decide or help; responsibility for driving the incident to resolution stays where it was unless command is explicitly handed over.

Change one factor: make the highest severity notify the director at declaration instead of after 2 hours. Leaders learn about the worst incidents immediately, and the path still keeps them informed rather than in command.

Source and limits: the example error-budget policy in The Site Reliability Workbook says a disagreement about the error-budget calculation should be escalated to the CTO to make a decision: https://sre.google/workbook/error-budget-policy/. leadership-metrics.essentialQuestion: A team is rewarded for lowering average latency. How can the average improve while the slowest requests stay just as slow, and which measure is harder to game?
leadership-metrics.verifiedBoundary: Operational metrics are useful when they describe outcomes or system health and do not reward gaming.
leadership-metrics.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: Measure the outcome you care about and watch for incentives your metric creates.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: Tracking ticket closure count alone rewards easy tickets; pairing it with reopen rate, age, satisfaction, and severity gives a fuller view. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented sample of 1,000 requests: 980 take 100 ms and 20 take 5,000 ms. Percentiles use the nearest-rank method, so the 99th percentile is the 990th fastest request. The distribution is illustrative.

Derivation: the mean is (980 × 100 + 20 × 5,000) / 1,000 = 198 ms, which looks healthy against a 300 ms goal. The median is 100 ms. The 99th percentile is 5,000 ms, because the 990th request falls among the 20 slow ones. The 20 users who waited 5 seconds are invisible in the average.

Independent check: speed up only the fast requests from 100 to 80 ms. The mean falls to (980 × 80 + 20 × 5,000) / 1,000 = 178.4 ms, an apparent improvement, while the 99th percentile stays at 5,000 ms. A target on the mean rewards that work; a target on the 99th percentile does not.
Misconception to reject: 'the average describes the typical user.' Here the typical user sees the median, 100 ms, and the users with problems see the tail; the mean describes neither group.

Change one factor: fix the slow path instead, so the 20 slow requests take 400 ms. The mean becomes (980 × 100 + 20 × 400) / 1,000 = 106 ms and the 99th percentile becomes 400 ms; both measures now agree that users are better off.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented service with a 99.9% availability objective measured over a rolling four-week (28-day) window. Derivation: the window has 28 × 24 × 60 = 40,320 minutes, so the budget is 0.1% of that, 40.32 minutes. Incident A uses 9 / 40.32 ≈ 22.3% of it and incident B about 14.9%. The policy requires a postmortem for any single incident that consumes more than 20% of the budget over four weeks, so A needs one and B does not.

Independent check: 20% of 40.32 minutes is 8.064 minutes; 9 is above it and 6 is below, which matches. After A and B the window holds 15 minutes, about 37.2% of the budget, so the service is within its objective. Incident C brings the total to 45 minutes, which exceeds the budget by 4.68 minutes.

Misconception to reject: 'the policy punishes the team.' The policy is agreed before any incident, so once the budget is exhausted the response is already decided: halt changes and releases except fixes for the most urgent issues and security until the service is back within its objective.

Change one factor: with a 99.5% objective, the four-week budget is 201.6 minutes, and the same 45 minutes uses about 22.3% of it, so there is no freeze. The objective chosen sets how much risk the team may take, which is why it is a product decision.

Source and limits: Appendix B of The Site Reliability Workbook, 'Example Error Budget Policy', halts all changes and releases other than P0 issues or security fixes when the service has exceeded its budget for the preceding four-week window, requires a postmortem for a single incident consuming more than 20% of the budget over four weeks and escalates disagreements about the calculation to the CTO: https://sre.google/workbook/error-budget-policy/. reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented service. The SLI is monthly availability; the internal SLO is 99.95%; the external SLA promises 99.9% and pays a 10% service credit when missed. The month has 31 days, and downtime is counted in whole minutes.

Independent check: 30 minutes lies between the two allowances, 22.32 and 44.64, so the same conclusion follows without computing a percentage. The internal objective has fired while customers are still within their agreement; that gap is the safety margin.

Misconception to reject: 'the SLO and the SLA are the same number.' The SLI is a measurement, the SLO is the target the team manages to and the SLA is a contract with consequences. Setting the internal objective tighter than the agreement gives the team room to respond before customers are owed anything.
Change one factor: with 50 minutes of downtime, availability is about 99.888%, below the agreement's 99.9%. On an invented $20,000 monthly fee, the 10% credit is $2,000.

Source and limits: chapter 4 of Google's Site Reliability Engineering book, 'Service Level Objectives', defines SLIs, SLOs and SLAs, describes an SLA as an explicit or implicit contract with users that includes consequences of meeting or missing its SLOs, and advises keeping a safety margin by using a tighter internal SLO than the one advertised: https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/. reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: one minute of measurements for an invented checkout API. The SRE book's four golden signals are latency (the time to service a request), traffic (the demand on the system), errors (the rate of failed requests) and saturation (how full the service is).

Derivation: traffic is 12,000 / 60 = 200 requests per second; errors are 180 / 12,000 = 1.5% of requests; latency at the 99th percentile is 850 ms, 350 ms over the 500 ms target; saturation is 92% of worker capacity.

Independent check: 12,000 − 180 = 11,820 requests succeeded, and 11,820 / 12,000 = 98.5%, consistent with a 1.5% error rate. Latency and errors describe what users experience now; saturation describes how close the service is to running out of capacity.

Misconception to reject: 'a busy worker pool is the outage.' High saturation is a warning, not user impact by itself; the SRE book's monitoring philosophy pages primarily on symptoms that users experience, such as the latency and error rates here.

Change one factor: double the traffic to 400 requests per second with the same capacity. The pool would need 92% × 2 = 184% of its capacity, so work queues, latency rises further and errors follow. Saturation was the signal that predicted this.

Source and limits: the four golden signals are defined in chapter 6 of Google's Site Reliability Engineering book, 'Monitoring Distributed Systems': https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/. One minute of data is a snapshot; percentiles and error rates should be read over windows that match the objective.

Change one factor: a smaller degradation of 0.6% errors for 6 hours is a burn rate of 6 and consumes 6 × 6 / 720 = 5% of the budget, the workbook's second paging threshold; at burn rate 1 over 3 days the workbook recommends a ticket instead of a page.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: three invented toil sources: manual certificate renewals (20 hours a month; automation costs 16 hours), access requests (10 hours a month; automation costs 30 hours) and restarting a job that leaks memory (6 hours a month; fixing the leak costs 24 hours and removes the restarts entirely). The quarter offers 40 engineering hours.

Derivation: payback time is the one-time cost divided by the monthly saving: 16 / 20 = 0.8 months for renewals, 30 / 10 = 3 months for access requests and 24 / 6 = 4 months for the leak fix. Renewals come first. Renewals plus the leak fix cost 16 + 24 = 40 hours and save 26 hours a month; renewals plus access requests would cost 46 hours, which does not fit.
Independent check: over the remaining two months of the quarter, renewals plus the leak fix save 2 × 26 = 52 hours for a 40-hour investment, while renewals alone save 2 × 20 = 40 hours for 16 hours.
Misconception to reject: 'automate every manual task.' Automating the restarts would keep the leak and add a restart system to maintain; fixing the leak removes the work and its cause.
Change one factor: if access requests grow to 25 hours a month, their payback falls to 30 / 25 = 1.2 months, and the ranking changes. Re-rank toil sources whenever their volumes change.

Source and limits: chapter 5 of Google's Site Reliability Engineering book, 'Eliminating Toil', sets the goal of keeping toil below 50% of each SRE's time and describes engineering work that reduces future toil: https://sre.google/sre-book/eliminating-toil/. Payback ignores the maintenance cost of the new automation.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: a single-site team covers on-call around the clock with two people on call at all times (primary and secondary), and each engineer may spend at most 25% of their time on call. Incidents are counted per 12-hour shift. The team details are invented.
Derivation: two people must always be on call, and each can cover at most a quarter of the time, so the rotation needs at least 2 / 0.25 = 8 engineers.
Independent check: with 8 engineers and week-long shifts, each engineer is primary or secondary for 2 of every 8 weeks, which is 25% of their time.

The SRE book reports that an incident takes about 6 hours on average once root-cause analysis, remediation and follow-up are included, which makes 2 incidents per 12-hour shift the practical maximum. Three incidents imply about 18 hours of work in a 12-hour shift, so follow-up work is being dropped.

Source and limits: chapter 11 of Google's Site Reliability Engineering book, 'Being On-Call', describes the 25% on-call limit, the 6-hour average incident cost, the maximum of 2 incidents per 12-hour shift and the dual-site minimum of six per site: https://sre.google/sre-book/being-on-call/. reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented service fails over its primary database a few times a year. Without a runbook, responders reconstruct the steps during the incident; with one, they follow steps written and rehearsed in advance.

Derivation: the SRE book reports that recording best practices ahead of time in a playbook produced roughly a 3x improvement in mean time to repair compared with improvising. Applied to this example, a failover that takes 90 minutes when improvised would take about 30 minutes with a runbook, if the same improvement held.

Independent check: the runbook's last test was 9 months ago, and since then the database version, the replication topology and the DNS provider have changed, a total of 3 changes that touch failover. Each untested change is a step that may no longer work, so the runbook should be treated as unverified.
Misconception to reject: 'a runbook is documentation, so writing it once is enough.' A runbook is a procedure; its value depends on being correct for the current system, which only a test can show.
Change one factor: schedule a failover drill after every change that touches the failover path and at least quarterly. A drill that finds a broken step turns a slow incident into a scheduled fix.

Source and limits: chapter 1 of Google's Site Reliability Engineering book reports that recording best practices in a playbook produces roughly a 3x improvement in MTTR compared with 'winging it': https://sre.google/sre-book/introduction/. That figure is Google's experience; the 90- and 30-minute values here are illustrative.
